title: UW Planetarium to Host 'Dome After Dark' Event, Meteor Shower Program During November
excerpt: The University of Wyoming Harry C. Vaughan Planetarium will provide another “Dome After Dark” event for campus and a program that highlights two upcoming meteor showers during November.
content:
The University of Wyoming Harry C. Vaughan Planetarium will provide another “Dome After Dark” event for campus and a program that highlights two upcoming meteor showers during November.

“We are excited to have our ‘Dome After Dark’ series of live music and visual arts Nov. 14. The show will feature multiple live musical and visual artists for our late-night ‘dance and create’ party,” says Max Gilbraith, the planetarium’s director. “The SCI-DIY makerspace will be open upstairs for activities including games and custom keepsakes, and snacks and refreshments are available throughout the evening.”

A Wyoming Skies program will focus on the fall constellations and an upcoming set of meteor showers -- the Taurids and Leonids, he adds.

To get tickets or receive more information about programs, email planetarium@uwyo.edu or leave a voicemail and a callback phone number at (307) 766-6506. Tickets are $5 for the public or online tickets, and $3 for students, senior citizens, veterans, first responders and those under 18. Seating is free for children under 5. Bulk tickets/gift cards are available at $2 each when 10 or more tickets are purchased.

Reservations or pre-purchase is not required, and walk-ins are welcome. Tickets can be purchased online with a credit card, reserved by email or voicemail, or purchased at the start of the show. Cash or check is accepted at the door. The planetarium, which seats 64, is in the basement of the Physical Sciences Building. Seating is on a first-come, first-served basis outside of designated ADA/wheelchair seating.

To pay for tickets with a credit card, go to www.uwyo.edu/uwplanetarium/ticket.aspx. For a group larger than six, email the planetarium for a private show at https://uwyo.sjc1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_bKuqIynOn7gFK2F. Tickets for private shows are the same as the public programs.

A film and special live talk for audiences will be featured each week. All programs are approximately an hour in length. As time allows, a portion of the show also may focus on a live sky tour or supporting information related to the film’s topic.

The November schedule is:

-- Friday, Nov. 6, 7 p.m.: “Black Holes.” Are black holes nature’s mistake or portals to the unknown? Physics can let us speculate about the nature of these bizarre structures, but astronomers are turning an improving eye toward these mysterious and fascinating objects.  

-- Friday, Nov. 6, 8:30 p.m.: “Laser Show: Daft Punk.” Enjoy a laser show featuring music from the electronic music band combined with custom laser art in 5.1 surround sound.

-- Saturday, Nov. 7, 2 p.m.: “Two Small Pieces of Glass: The Amazing Telescope,” a full-dome movie and a star talk. Attendees will learn about the history of the telescope, from Galileo’s modifications to a child’s spyglass -- using two small pieces of glass -- to the launch of the NASA/European Space Agency Hubble Space Telescope and the future of astronomy.

-- Saturday, Nov. 7, 7 p.m.: “5,000 Eyes: Mapping the Universe with DESI,” a full-dome movie and a star talk. The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) is creating the most detailed map of our nearby universe. Installed on the Nicholas U. Mayall Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in southern Arizona, DESI’s 5,000 independently operated robots can measure the light from thousands of galaxies at once. Explore the science, instrument and people behind this global endeavor.

-- Saturday, Nov. 7, 8:30 p.m.: “Laser Show: Best of Pink Floyd.” Enjoy a laser show featuring music from the classic progressive and psychedelic rock band combined with custom laser art in 5.1 surround sound.

-- Tuesday, Nov. 10, 7 p.m.: “Wyoming Skies: Taurids and Leonids Meteor Showers.” The Taurids are a complex shower made up of two main components: the annual component, which peaked Oct. 14, and the fireball-swarm component, which peaks Nov. 5. The Southern Taurids are rich in fireballs and are often responsible for an increased number of fireball reports from September through November. The Northern Taurids peak Wednesday-Thursday, Nov. 11-12.

The Leonids are best known for producing meteor storms in 1833, 1866, 1966, 1999, 2001 and 2002. These outbursts are best seen when the parent object, comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is near perihelion. It is not fresh material from the comet that can be viewed, but debris from earlier returns that happens to be most dense at the same time. Earth will not encounter any dense clouds of debris until 2099. The Leonids peak Monday-Tuesday, Nov. 16-17.

After the planetarium show finishes at 8 p.m., informal telescope observing on the rooftop of the Physical Sciences Building at the STAR Observatory will be available, weather permitting.

-- Friday, Nov. 13, 7 p.m.: “Size of the Universe -- Voyager at One Light Day.” Ever wondered how far away the moon really is? Or what our solar system would look like if the sun was 100 times larger? Explore the universe in bite-sized chunks, in distance scales we can understand and learn the true size of the universe. The ongoing distance record of the Voyager 1 spacecraft, launched in 1977, is approaching one light-day this month. Attendees will see just how far, and close, that really is in the scale of the cosmos.

-- Friday, Nov. 13, 8:30 p.m.: “Laser Show: Laser Legends.” Enjoy a laser show featuring various musical legends combined with custom laser art in 5.1 surround sound. The music of Johnny Cash, Jim Morrison, Whitney Houston, Michael Jackson, Prince, John Lennon, David Bowie, Elvis Presley and Jimi Hendrix will be featured.

-- Saturday, Nov. 14, 2 p.m.: “Messengers of Time and Space,” a full-dome movie and a star talk. The film is designed to illuminate the imminent revolution in astronomy driven by time-domain and multi-messenger observations. This immersive experience invites audiences to explore the dynamic cosmos and witness the transformative impact of real-time data on our understanding of the universe. The film was created by the National Science Foundation’s NOIRLab.

-- Saturday, Nov. 14, 7 p.m.: “Dark Biosphere,” a full-dome movie and a star talk. Deep beneath the Earth’s crust, hundreds of meters or kilometers below the surface -- with no light, no air and very little water, in pores and fissures of hard rock -- scientists have found an enormous biodiversity of micro-organisms that thrive in extreme conditions in an area known as the dark biosphere. This film is narrated by actor Viggo Mortensen.

-- Saturday, Nov. 14, 9 p.m.-1 a.m.: “Dome After Dark: Dance and Create.” Lose yourself in a 360-degree universe of music, lasers and creative play. The UW Planetarium dome becomes a living canvas -- part dance floor and part immersive art installation, with pop-up makerspace activities, interactive visuals and plenty of space to create and connect. Supplies will be provided for attendees to make something creative and explore the technology in the SciDIY Makerspace. Doors open at 8:30 p.m., and the cost is $15. Light refreshments will be served.

 -- Friday, Nov. 20: The planetarium will be closed due to the evening home football game between UW and the University of New Mexico.

-- Saturday, Nov. 21, 2 p.m.: “The Great Solar System Adventure,” a full-dome movie and a star talk. Join showman extraordinaire “The Great Schiaparelli” as he takes the audience on a death-defying, space-time adventure within his wondrous observatorium. From the sun-scorched surface of Mercury to the icy expanses of Pluto and beyond, the audience will be subjected to the myriad dangers and wonders of our solar system.

-- Saturday, Nov. 21, 7 p.m.: “We Are Stars,” a full-dome movie and a star talk. What are we made of? Where did it all come from? Explore the secrets of our cosmic chemistry and our explosive origins. Connect life on Earth to the evolution of the universe by following the formation of hydrogen atoms to the synthesis of carbon, and the molecules for life. This film is narrated by Andy Serkis.

-- Saturday, Nov 21, 8:30 p.m.: “Liquid Sky: Psychedelic Rock.” Enjoy a custom playlist of “out-of-this-world” psychedelic rock music in 5.1 surround sound. The 4K-resolution planetarium sky melts and becomes a canvas of color, patterns and movement with cutting-edge music visualization software and live VJ talent.

-- Tuesday, Nov. 24-Sunday, Nov. 29: The planetarium will be closed due to the Thanksgiving holiday break.

For more detailed descriptions of all programs, go to www.uwyo.edu/physics/planetarium/schedule.html.
